scenes.name: Sugar Hill Records y Rapper’s Delight
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Sylvia Robinson, la «madre del hip hop», venía del R&B: Little Sylvia, el dúo Mickey & Sylvia («Love Is Strange», 1956), la producción del «It’s Gonna Work Out Fine» de Ike & Tina, el sello All Platinum con su marido Joe (con supuestos lazos mafiosos) y su propio éxito «Pillow Talk» (1973). Arruinada, vio a Lovebug Starski en Harlem World en 1979 y quiso grabar aquello; con Morris Levy fundaron Sugar Hill. Su hijo la llevó a una pizzería de Nueva Jersey donde Big Bank Hank, mánager de los Cold Crush, hizo una audición en su coche junto a Master Gee y Wonder Mike: la Sugarhill Gang. Sobre una recreación de «Good Times» de Chic grabaron quince minutos de rimas que una radio de St. Louis, WESL, se atrevió a poner: «Rapper’s Delight» inundó el mundo en otoño de 1979, dejó en anécdota el «King Tim III» de Fatback y demostró que el hip hop era negocio. En el Bronx sonaba a imitación higienizada: Hank rapeaba las rimas de Grandmaster Caz («I’m the C-A-S-AN, the O-V-A»), un estribillo de Hollywood y una frase de Rahiem; «hizo retroceder el hip hop cinco años» (Charlie Chase). Para Kool Moe Dee, sin Sugar Hill quizá no habría industria. La casa no pagaba bien a sus artistas, y su banda (Skip Alexander, Doug Wimbish, Duke Bootee) tocaba los temas. En Harlem, Bobby Robinson y su sello Enjoy ficharon a Flash, los Funky 4 + 1 y los Treacherous Three.

scenes.name: Sweet funk: el soul sexual
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Tras Let’s Get It On, «Me and Mrs. Jones» de Billy Paul y «Let’s Stay Together» de Al Green llegó una nueva hornada de cantantes sensuales. Barry White, con su orquesta de estudio sobre una sección rítmica de R&B, unió la elegancia occidental y la sensualidad negra: un lujo negro impensable diez años antes. Los Moments («Sexy Mama»), Main Ingredient, los Miracles («Do It Baby»), Leon Haywood («I Want’a Do Something Freaky to You», base de «Nothin’ but a G Thang» de Dr. Dre) o New Birth mezclaron psicodelia, melodía y funk sucio; Sylvia Robinson susurró «Pillow Talk» (1973) y Major Harris remató «Love Won’t Let Me Wait» con un orgasmo simulado.

scenes.name: Hip hop neoyorquino
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Con la música negra popular muerta estéticamente, el alma del pueblo pasó al underground: un funk ruidoso, áspero y tenso, demasiado desesperado para la radio negra. Los breaks de DJ Kool Herc en las fiestas de barrio del Bronx, Jazzy Jay, Afrika Bambaataa, DJ Hollywood, Grandmaster Flash y Eddie Cheeba convirtieron la mezcla de discos en arte: los chavales dejaron las bandas por dos platos, el scratch y los breaks repetidos, un collage posmoderno de toda la música grabada sobre un ritmo funky. Sylvia Robinson grabó en 1979 «Rapper’s Delight» de la Sugarhill Gang y fichó a Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five, cuya «The Message» (1982), con Melle Mel, dio voz a los sin voz como no se oía desde «What’s Going On»; siguieron «White Lines» o «New York, New York». Las cajas de ritmos dieron un funk industrial y minimalista (el bombo 808, «Five Minutes of Funk» de Whodini), y Run-D.M.C. («It’s Like That», «Rock Box», «King of Rock», «Walk This Way» con Aerosmith en Raising Hell, 1986) asaltó la radio rock, seguidos por los Beastie Boys.
scenes.family: Hip hop, go-go y funk de los noventa

podcast.title: Acquisition of "Love Is Strange" Share
podcast.body: According to Bo Diddley, he sold his share in the song "Love Is Strange" to Sylvia sometime in the early 1960s, a move that aligns with her reputation for making "very wise business decisions." "According to Deadly, he also later sold his own share in the song to Sylvia, sometime in the early 60s. This may well be the case, because Sylvia Van Tapool went on to become a very, very successful businessman, who made a lot of very wise business decisions."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Business Acumen and Ambition
podcast.body: Sylvia possessed a "razor-sharp business mind" and a "huge amount of ambition and a desire for stardom," contrasting sharply with Mickey Baker's more private and studious nature. "Sylvia had a razor-sharp business mind, a huge amount of ambition and a desire for stardom."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 49: "Love is Strange" by Mickey and Sylvia

podcast.title: Day Job as a Typist
podcast.body: By the age of 20, Sylvia was working as a typist, struggling to make a living as a singer despite taking guitar lessons from Mickey Baker and becoming "pretty good." "By the time she was 20, Sylvia was holding down a day job as a typist, trying and failing to earn enough money to live on as a singer, but she'd been taking guitar lessons from Mickey Baker and had got pretty good."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 49: "Love is Strange" by Mickey and Sylvia

podcast.title: Discovery of The Sugar Hill Gang
podcast.body: Sylvia Robinson discovered Big Hank, a member of The Sugar Hill Gang, through a tip from her son at Krispy Krust Pizza in New York. She then recruited the other two members by driving around and asking rappers if they were interested in recording rap over the music of Chic's "Good Times." This unconventional method led to the formation of the group and the recording of "Rapper's Delight" in just 14 minutes. "Legend has that Sylvia discovered Big Hank on a tip from her son at Krispy Krust Pizza in New York."

podcast.title: Early Career as "Little Sylvia"
podcast.body: Sylvia began her recording career at the age of 13, using the stage name "Little Sylvia," inspired by Little Esther, who also recorded for Savoy Records. "Sylvia was only 13 when she started her career, using the name Little Sylvia, inspired by Little Esther, who like her was making records for Savoy records."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 49: "Love is Strange" by Mickey and Sylvia

podcast.title: Founder of Sugar Hill Records
podcast.body: Sylvia Robinson founded Sugar Hill Records with the intention of recording a rap record. She faced challenges in finding rap artists willing to be recorded, as rap was primarily viewed as a live performance art, and many doubted its commercial viability on vinyl. Her perseverance led to the discovery and recording of The Sugar Hill Gang. "Sylvia Robinson knew she wanted to record a rap record, but she was having a really hard time finding a rap artist who would agree to be recorded."

podcast.title: Founding All Platinum Records
podcast.body: After the duo with Mickey Baker split, Sylvia took a few years off to have children before establishing her own record label, All Platinum. For this label, she wrote and produced a number of proto-disco hits for other artists. "After a few years off to have kids after the duos split up, she set up her own record label, All Platinum."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 49: "Love is Strange" by Mickey and Sylvia

podcast.title: Lead Guitar and Backing Vocals for Ike & Tina Turner
podcast.body: On Ike & Tina Turner's hit "It's Gonna Work Out Fine," Sylvia played the lead guitar part and joined The Ikettes on backing vocals, making the record essentially a Mickey & Sylvia production with Tina Turner as guest vocalist. "Sylvia played the lead guitar part while Mickey did the spoken Ag vocals, which Ag would do live. Sylvia also joined the Ag Kets on backing vocals."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 49: "Love is Strange" by Mickey and Sylvia

podcast.title: Musical Background
podcast.body: Sylvia Robinson was a member of the duo Mickey and Sylvia in the late 1950s, known for their song "Love Is Strange." Her past experience in the music industry gave her insight into creating popular music. "You might know her from Mickey and Sylvia from the late 50s, or if you remember that scene in dirty dancing when Baby and Johnny were dancing to love his strange, she was that Sylvia."

podcast.title: Pivotal Figure in Hip-Hop
podcast.body: Sylvia Robinson is described as becoming to hip-hop what Sam Phillips was to rock and roll. In 1979, with financing from her husband Joe Robinson's gangster friend Morris Levy, she was more responsible than anyone from the first wave of rock and roll stars for recognizing the commercial potential in hip-hop. "Because Sylvia Robinson, who had been little Sylvia, and the woman calling her lover boy, became to hip-hop, what Sam Phillips was to rock and roll."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Possible Co-writer of "It's Gonna Work Out Fine" (as Sylvia McKinney)
podcast.body: Sylvia Robinson (then Sylvia Van Topoele) is possibly the same person as Sylvia McKinney, who is credited as a co-writer on "It's Gonna Work Out Fine," a song Mickey & Sylvia suggested for Ike & Tina Turner. "The other credited co-writer is one Sylvia McKinney, who some sources suggest is the same person as Sylvia Van Topool, who had by this point married Joe Robinson and changed her name to Sylvia Robinson."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Relationship with Joe Robinson and Management
podcast.body: Sylvia started dating Joe Robinson, a man with connections to gangsters, who decided to become her manager to boost her floundering career by forming a duo with Mickey Baker. "But then Sylvia started dating a man named Joe Robinson. Joe Robinson was involved in some way with gangsters."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Unsuccessful Early Recordings
podcast.body: Her initial recordings on Savoy and Jubilee Records were unsuccessful, characterized by a "strange mix of different styles" that lacked a coherent or distinctive sound necessary to establish her as a star. "She had recorded several unsuccessful tracks on Savoy and Jubilee records."
